            How these figures are worked out

            Suburb prices are 12-month medians (each point covers the year to that month); areas use 3-month medians. Suburb rents are by postcode. Area sales are counted by quarter. Sale-by-sale charts use contract dates; the price and land filters apply to them (land to houses only), and sales over four times or under a quarter of their suburb’s typical price that year are left out (development sites, part shares). Candles take each month’s first, highest, lowest and last sale: these are different homes, so a candle shows spread and timing, not one price moving.

            Drag to move through time, scroll to zoom, drag the price scale to stretch it and the date scale to zoom, double-click the chart (or press auto, bottom right) to fit the data again, and double-click a scale to reset just that one. Click a drawing to select it, drag its handles to change it, Delete to remove it. Start typing anywhere on the chart to change the main series.

            Buy or rent, on your numbers

            Four steps: what you can borrow, the home, the loan, then buying against renting for every year of the loan. Shorthand like 250k or 1.2m works. Nothing leaves this browser.

            A calculator, not advice. It shows what happens to your money under the assumptions on this page, all of which you can change. It doesn't know your full situation and doesn't recommend any property, loan or lender. Results are estimates, not a forecast or a lender's assessment. Don't rely on them to make a decision: get advice from a licensed financial adviser first. Step 4 shows every year in today's dollars, so a figure 20 years out means what that money would buy now.             No listings. No asking prices. Just what sold.

            Every figure here is a recorded sale or a lodged rental bond from NSW Government records. Nothing you type leaves your browser.
            How the numbers workMethods, definitions and what to watch for
            Buy or rent
            Your budget compares your net worth, year by year, from buying against keeping the rent you pay now and saving the difference (or just saving, if you pay no rent). For an investment, both sides keep paying your own rent; one buys the property and lets it out, the other keeps the cash in savings. Savings earn interest at the savings rate, taxed every year at the lower earner's marginal rate. Price growth blends the suburb's 10-year record with its region's, capped. Loan principal counts as saving, not cost. Every input is under More assumptions.
            Borrowing and deposit
            A rough guide, not a lender's assessment: after-tax income less living costs and other repayments must cover the loan at your rate plus a buffer. Lenders use their own living-cost floors, so yours may come out lower. Your cash pays stamp duty and costs first; the rest is deposit. Under 20% deposit, approximate mortgage insurance (1% to 5% of the loan) is added, unless you tick the 5% Deposit Scheme (first home buyers, up to $1.5m in Sydney). First home buyer duty uses the NSW exemption to $800k and an approximate concession to $1m.
            Price changes and falls
            For an area (Greater Sydney, regional NSW, all of NSW, or a named area such as Newcastle or the Central Coast) we compare 3-month medians: the middle price of every sale that settled in a three-month window. Three months is long enough to steady the figure and short enough to turn within about a month of the market. A 12-month median runs six or seven months late: in 2022 Sydney house prices peaked in January, but the 12-month median didn't peak until August. "From the peak" is the latest three months against the highest three-month median in the last three years. "On a year ago" is the latest three months against the same three months a year earlier, so the season is the same. "Last 3 months" is against the three months before; it reacts fastest but moves with the season (spring is usually dearer), so read it as a direction. An area needs at least 100 sales in three months; with fewer, sampling alone can swing the median by 10% or more, so the headline falls back to suburb figures. Suburbs use 12 months of sales instead, because most have too few sales in three months for a reliable median; their colours on the map turn later as a result. No figure is adjusted for the season or for the mix of homes sold.
            Prices and the time slider
            Each month shows the median of the 12 months of sales before it, so the map moves smoothly but turns a few months late. A chosen period compares the 12-month median at its start and end. Sales count once they settle, usually 6 to 7 weeks after contract, so figures trail the market by about that much. Suburbs marked "new" have under 10 years of sales and use their region's growth.
            What's left out of medians
            One price covering several homes (a developer buying a row of houses), and sales over 5 times or under a fifth of the suburb's typical price that year (development sites, family transfers). Both stay on the map: choose "Unusual prices" in the sales bar. Suburbs with fewer than 15 sales are left out of comparisons, because one sale can swing their median.
            Houses and units
            A sale is a unit when it's on a strata title, so most villas and many townhouses count as units. Rents come from bond lodgements by postcode, from 2021, where townhouses are grouped with houses. Lots later split into a duplex or units are marked as subdivided, with no value estimate.
            Before 2001
            The 1990 to 2000 records have no settlement date (estimated at contract plus 6 weeks) and no residence or strata flags, so they're classified from zoning and the land description.
